claim: The Grotta della Bàsura is a large and deep cave that has produced some of the most important Italian Palaeolithic discoveries of the twentieth century.
source: Discovered in 1950, the hypogeal part of the 'Grotta della Bàsura' is a large and deep cave that has produced some of the most important Italian Palaeolithic discoveries of the twentieth century (Chiappella, 1952; Tongiorgi and Lamboglia, 1954; Blanc, 1960; Lamboglia, 1960; Giacobini, 2008)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to historical literature documenting the cave's discoveries

claim: The cave contains traces of human activity, especially footprints, dating back to 14 ky cal. BP.
source: Discovered in 1950, the hypogeal part of the 'Grotta della Bàsura' is a large and deep cave that has produced some of the most important Italian Palaeolithic discoveries of the twentieth century (Chiappella, 1952; Tongiorgi and Lamboglia, 1954; Blanc, 1960; Lamboglia, 1960; Giacobini, 2008) consisting of traces of human activity, especially footprints, dating back to 14 ky cal. BP.
evidence: Supported by radiometric dating data presented in Table 1 and cited literature

claim: Until 1890, only the atrial part of the cavity was known where Neolithic and late Roman archaeological finds had been unearthed.
source: Up till 1890 only the atrial part of the cavity was known where Neolithic and late Roman archaeological finds had been unearthed (Maineri, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to historical archaeological work

claim: The cave opening is situated at 186 m a.s.l. about 1 km north of Toirano, Savona, Italy.
source: The cave opening is situated at 186 m a.s.l. about 1 km north of Toirano (Savona, Italy - 436253.433 E; 4887689.739 N)
evidence: Provides specific geographic coordinates and elevation data

claim: The cave extends 890 m into Mount S. Pietro with an elevation difference of +20/−22 m relative to the entrance.
source: extends 890 m into Mount S. Pietro with an elevation difference of +20/−22 m relative to that of the entrance (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements and visualization in Figure 1

claim: The inner rooms became accessible in 1950 after the rupture of a stalagmite column that had prevented access to the cave.
source: The inner rooms became accessible in 1950, after the rupture of a stalagmite column, placed a few dozen meters from the entrance, that prevented any access to the cave (Tongiorgi and Lamboglia, 1954; Blanc, 1960; Lamboglia, 1960).
evidence: Supported by multiple historical citations

claim: Virginia Chiappella was the first scholar to visit the site soon after its discovery and identified several bones of Ursus spelaeus and traces of animal and human frequentation.
source: The exceptional prehistoric and paleontological value of the cave was firstly recognized by Virginia Chiappella (Chiappella, 1952) who was the first scholar to visit the site soon after its discovery. Chiappella identified several bones of Ursus spelaeus and traces both of animal and human frequentation (footprints, charcoals, digital tracks, lumps of clay adhering to the walls) in different areas of the cave within approximately 350 m of the entrance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiappella's original work

claim: Destruction of most of the ichnological record occurred as a result of uncontrolled cave visits by local villagers and tourists following media reports.
source: Regrettably, destruction of most of the ichnological record occurred as a result of uncontrolled cave visits by local villagers and tourists lured to the remarkable discovery as a result of media reports (Blanc et al., 1960; De Lumley and Giacobini, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations documenting the destruction

claim: The first study of human footprints from the Cave of Bàsura was conducted by Pales in 1960 based on original images and 13 plaster casts.
source: The first study of human footprints from the Cave of Bàsura was conducted by Pales (1960), based on original images and 13 plaster casts of the best-preserved specimens from various sectors of the cave.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pales' original work

claim: Pales considered that the footprints were made by 'Neanderthal-type' producers based on analysis of bone architecture and apparent relationship with Ursus spelaeus remains.
source: Analysis of the bone architecture of the footprint makers and the apparent relationship with remains of Ursus spelaeus, led the author to consider that the footprints were made by 'Neanderthal-type' producers.
evidence: Based on inference from Pales' analysis as cited

claim: Subsequent analysis placed the prehistoric visitation of the Bàsura in the Upper Palaeolithic, between 12,000 and 14,000 years uncal BP.
source: Subsequent analysis (de Lumley and Vicino, 1984), accompanied by radiometric dating, placed the prehistoric visitation of the Bàsura in the Upper Palaeolithic, between 12,000 and 14,000 years uncal BP (de Lumley and Vicino, 1984; De Lumley and Giacobini, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to radiometric dating studies

claim: Dating of charred wood fragments found on the trampled surface provided an age for cave visitation at 12,340 years ± 160 years BP.
source: Dating of charred wood fragments found on the trampled surface provided a more precise age for cave visitation at 12,340 years ± 160 years BP (Molleson et al., 1972; Molleson, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to radiometric dating studies

claim: Blanc proposed that the inner room called 'Sala dei Misteri' was reached by multiple individuals, including a juvenile.
source: Based on the ichnological study of Pales, Blanc proposed that the inner room called 'Sala dei Misteri' was reached by multiple individuals, including a juvenile.
evidence: Based on inference from ichnological evidence as cited

claim: Blanc described a group of seven human footprints identified by heel tracks positioned only a few centimeters from the main wall of the chamber to which numerous lumps of clay were attached.
source: Blanc (1960) described, from the same room, a group of seven human footprints identified by heel tracks positioned only a few centimeters from the main wall of the chamber to which numerous lumps of clay were attached.
evidence: Supported by citation to Blanc's description

claim: The close association of footprints with lumps of clay resulted in it being considered the result of initiation rites involving young hunters.
source: The close association of the footprints with lumps of clay resulted in it being considered the result of initiation rites involving young hunters.
evidence: Based on interpretation from cited work

claim: A total of 180 footprints and traces sensu lato were recorded and studied.
source: A total of 180 footprints and traces sensu lato were recorded and studied (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary file

claim: Among the traces are digit and handprints on the clay-rich floor, and smears from hands dirtied with charcoal on the side walls of the cave.
source: In addition to footprints (Figure 2), among the traces are digit and handprints on the clay-rich floor, and smears from hands dirtied with charcoal on the side walls of the cave (Figure 3) (Giannotti, 2008).
evidence: Supported by figures showing the traces and citation

claim: A paleo-archaeological excavation was performed in 2016 in the 'Sala dei Misteri' which highlighted the total absence of archaeological material.
source: A paleo-archaeological excavation was performed in 2016 in the 'Sala dei Misteri'. This survey highlighted the total absence of archaeological material but led to the recovery, on the trampled palaeosurface, of numerous charcoal remains with bundles of Pinus t. sylvestris/mugo originally used to illuminate the cave.
evidence: Based on excavation data from 2016

claim: The 2016 excavation led to the recovery of numerous charcoal remains with bundles of Pinus t. sylvestris/mugo originally used to illuminate the cave.
source: A paleo-archaeological excavation was performed in 2016 in the 'Sala dei Misteri'. This survey highlighted the total absence of archaeological material but led to the recovery, on the trampled palaeosurface, of numerous charcoal remains with bundles of Pinus t. sylvestris/mugo originally used to illuminate the cave.
evidence: Based on excavation data and identification of wood species

claim: New radiometric dating on charcoal samples constrains the exploration of the cave to the late Upper Palaeolithic, between 12,310 ± 60 and 12,370 ± 60 BP, that is from about 14,700 to 14,000 cal BP.
source: New radiometric dating on these charcoal samples constrains the exploration of the cave to the late Upper Palaeolithic, between 12,310 ± 60 and 12,370 ± 60 BP, that is from about 14,700 to 14,000 cal BP (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by radiometric dating data presented in Table 1

claim: Different sized bear and Canidae incertae sedis footprints are ubiquitously present and are often associated with human prints.
source: Moreover, different sized bear and Canidae incertae sedis footprints are ubiquitously present (Figure 4), and are often associated with human prints.
evidence: Supported by Figure 4 showing the footprints

claim: The available data regarding the footprints attributed to 'canids' suggest a very reduced number of individuals and a close association with the human prints.
source: The available data regarding the footprints attributed to 'canids' suggest a very reduced number of individuals and a close association with the human prints.
evidence: Based on analysis of ichnological data

claim: The ichnological association of Bàsura could prove crucial to shed new light on dog domestication in the Upper Paleolithic.
source: Should ongoing studies (Avanzini et al in prep.) confirm that the ichnnological association of Bàsura could prove crucial to shed new light on dog domestication in the Upper Paleolithic (Morey and Jeger, 2015; Perri, 2016; Lupo, 2017; Janssens et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative statement about potential implications, supported by citations to dog domestication literature

claim: Ursus sp. hibernation areas are still recognizable with well-preserved nests of both cubs and adult bears.
source: Ursus sp. hibernation areas are still recognizable with well-preserved nests of both cubs and adult bears.
evidence: Based on direct observation of cave features

claim: Footprints are preserved in several areas of the cave, particularly in the innermost chamber ('Sala dei Misteri') and in the main gallery ('Corridoio delle impronte').
source: Footprints are preserved in several areas of the cave, particularly in the innermost chamber ('Sala dei Misteri') and in the main gallery ('Corridoio delle impronte' – Footprints Corridor), which is divided into two corridors at different elevations of about 5 m (referred to as the lower and upper corridor, respectively) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1 showing cave layout

claim: The main gallery is divided into two corridors at different elevations of about 5 m, referred to as the lower and upper corridor.
source: Footprints are preserved in several areas of the cave, particularly in the innermost chamber ('Sala dei Misteri') and in the main gallery ('Corridoio delle impronte' – Footprints Corridor), which is divided into two corridors at different elevations of about 5 m (referred to as the lower and upper corridor, respectively) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1 and measurement data

claim: Flooding dynamics and cave geometry produced two different situations for sediment deposition and transport inside the cave.
source: Flooding dynamics and cave geometry produced two different situations for sediment deposition and transport inside the cave.
evidence: Based on geological interpretation of sedimentary features

claim: Detrital sediment comprising silty clay and well-sorted sandy sediment are most abundant on the floor of the 'Sala dei Misteri'.
source: Detrital sediment comprising silty clay and well-sorted sandy sediment are most abundant on the floor of the 'Sala dei Misteri'.
evidence: Based on sedimentological analysis

claim: The sandy fraction comprises allogenic, surface-derived siliciclastic sediment.
source: The sandy fraction comprises allogenic, surface-derived siliciclastic sediment.
evidence: Based on sedimentological analysis and interpretation

claim: The 'Sala dei Misteri' appears to have undergone episodic filling and erosion as a result of catastrophic storms.
source: The 'Sala dei Misteri' appears to have undergone episodic filling and erosion as a result of catastrophic storms.
evidence: Based on interpretation of sedimentary features

claim: Sediment in the 'Corridoio delle impronte' comprises a large mud fraction and includes many coarse lithic fragments which are mainly carbonates (calcite and dolomite), suggesting an autogenic origin.
source: Sediment in the 'Corridoio delle impronte' comprises a large mud fraction and includes many coarse lithic fragments which are mainly carbonates (calcite and dolomite), suggesting an autogenic origin.
evidence: Based on sedimentological analysis and interpretation of origin

claim: At the time when humans and other large mammals left their traces the cave substrate differed in different areas of the cave, with some areas having plastic substrate and others waterlogged or submerged.
source: At the time when humans and other large mammals left their traces the cave substrate differed in different areas of the cave. In some areas, the substrate was plastic and in other areas it was waterlogged or submerged.
evidence: Based on inference from footprint preservation characteristics

claim: Differing moisture content of the substrate accounts for the variable preservation of detail of the tracks.
source: Differing moisture content of the substrate accounts for the variable preservation of detail of the tracks (e.g. registration of plantar arch, heel and metatarsal regions, digit tips, track walls), particularly of the associated extra-morphologies (e.g. expulsion rims, slipping traces).
evidence: Based on inference from observed preservation patterns

claim: The surface of the substrate and the footprints are cross-cut by mud cracks, suggesting a loss of moisture in sediments after trampling.
source: The surface of the substrate and the footprints are cross-cut by mud cracks, suggesting a loss of moisture in sediments after trampling.
evidence: Based on observation of mud cracks and inference about drying

claim: Carbonate crusts (comprising both calcite and dolomite) cover many of the footprints in areas subjected to more intense dripping.
source: Carbonate crusts (comprising both calcite and dolomite) cover many of the footprints in areas subjected to more intense dripping.
evidence: Based on mineralogical analysis and observation

claim: Iron and manganese oxide coatings were found in the crust, probably due to repeated immersion in ponded water.
source: Iron and manganese oxide coatings were found in the crust, probably due to repeated immersion in ponded water.
evidence: Based on geochemical analysis and interpretation of formation mechanism

claim: Geometric morphometry performed on human footprints highlighted five main morphotypes indicating a possible minimum number of five individuals entering the cave.
source: Geometric morphometry performed on human footprints highlighted five main morphotypes (hereafter Morphs.) indicating a possible minimum number of five individuals entering the cave (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by geometric morphometric analysis and Figure 5

claim: The minimum number of five individuals is confirmed by the construction of morphological groups reconstructed through the overlapping of footprints that show a variability of less than 2% of the main parameters.
source: This number is confirmed by the construction of morphological groups (Table 2) reconstructed through the overlapping of footprints that show a variability of less than 2% of the main parameters.
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis data in Table 2

claim: Morphotype 1 includes footprints with a length of 13.55 ± 0.49 cm showing characters indicative of an early ontogenetic stage of the producer.
source: Morph. 1 includes footprints with a length of 13.55 ± 0.49 cm showing characters indicative of an early ontogenetic stage of the producer, such as digit traces and the heel area proportionally wider than those of the longer tracks.
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements and interpretation

claim: Morphotype 2 has a length of 17 cm and is distinguished from Morphotype 1 on the basis of a more pronounced plantar arch.
source: Morph. 2, with a length of 17 cm, is distinguished from Morph. one on the basis of a more pronounced plantar arch.
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements and morphological comparison

claim: Morphotype 3 comprises footprints 20.83 ± 0.51 cm in length.
source: Morph. 3 comprises footprints 20.83 ± 0.51 cm in length (Figure 5 and Table 3).
evidence: Supported by measurements in Table 3 and Figure 5

claim: The plantar area of Morphotype 3 is characterized by a very pronounced medial embayment corresponding with a strongly convex external margin.
source: The plantar area is characterized by a very pronounced medial embayment. This corresponds with a strongly convex external margin, as is shared together with a strong adduction of digit I trace, an overall larger divarication of digit traces and a consistent separation between adjacent digits II-III and IV-V.
evidence: Based on morphological analysis of footprints

claim: Morphotype 4 is represented by larger footprints (22.80 ± 0.42 cm in overall length) with roughly straight medial and lateral margins and a medial embayment less marked than that of Morphotype 3.
source: Morph. 4 (Figures 5 and 6) is represented by larger footprints (22.80 ± 0,42 cm in overall length) with roughly straight medial and lateral margins and a medial embayment less marked than that of Morph. 3.
evidence: Supported by measurements and morphological description with figures

claim: Morphotype 5 includes footprints of 25.73 ± 0.45 cm in overall length and slightly concave margins, with a variably pronounced plantar embayment.
source: Morph. 5 (Figures 5 and 7) includes footprints of 25.73 ± 0.45 cm in overall length and slightly concave margins, with a variably pronounced plantar embayment.
evidence: Supported by measurements and morphological description with figures

claim: The footprints of Morphotype 5 are generally more robust and stockier than those of Morphotypes 3 and 4.
source: The footprints of Morph. 5 are generally more robust and stockier than those of Morphs. 3 and 4, sharing with Morph. 4 the straight, forwardly oriented digit tips, and with Morph. 3 an adducted digit I trace.
evidence: Based on morphological comparison

claim: Plantigrade tracks enabled estimation of stature, weight and ontogenetic stage of the producers based on biometric measurements.
source: Plantigrade tracks enabled us to estimate stature, weight and ontogenetic stage of the producers based on biometric measurements (Table 3) and the adopted formulas (see Methods).
evidence: Based on biometric analysis using established formulas

claim: The group of human track producers entering the cave comprised: a three-year-old child about 88 cm tall (Morphotype 1); a child at least 6 years old and about 110 cm tall (Morphotype 2); a pre-adolescent, between 8 and 11 years old, about 135 cm tall (Morphotype 3); a sub-adult to adult about 148 cm tall (Morphotype 4); and an adult about 167 cm tall (Morphotype 5).
source: The group of human track producers entering the cave comprised: a three-year-old child about 88 cm tall (Morph. 1); a child at least 6 years old and about 110 cm tall (Morph. 2); a pre-adolescent, between 8 and 11 years old, about 135 cm tall (Morph. 3); a sub-adult to adult about 148 cm tall (Morph. 4); and an adult about 167 cm tall (Morph. 5).
evidence: Based on biometric analysis and age estimation from footprint measurements

claim: The stature estimate for Morphotype 5 is further supported by the length of the tibia derived from the available kneeling traces.
source: Estimate of the stature for the Morph. 5 is further supported by the length of the tibia derived from the available kneeling traces (see Methods).
evidence: Based on anatomical measurements from kneeling traces

claim: The results concerning Morphotypes 4 and 5, which are referred to adult individuals, are in agreement with the average stature of European Upper Palaeolithic people (162.4 ± 4.6 cm for males and 153.9 ± 4.3 cm for females).
source: Our results concerning Morphs. 4 and 5, which are referred to adult individuals, are in agreement with the average stature of European Upper Palaeolithic people (162.4 ± 4.6 cm for males and 153.9 ± 4.3 cm for females) (Villotte et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with published data on Upper Palaeolithic stature

claim: Body mass estimates derived from footprint parameters suggest slender and muscular body proportions for all the trackmakers.
source: Body mass estimates derived from footprint parameters suggests slender and muscular body proportions for all the trackmakers.
evidence: Based on body mass calculations from footprint measurements

claim: Arch angle and footprint morphology suggests a male as the probable trackmaker of the largest footprint group.
source: Arch angle and footprint morphology suggests a male as the probable trackmaker of the largest footprint group.
evidence: Based on morphological analysis and comparison with sex-specific characteristics

claim: The gender is difficult to infer for morphotypes 1, 2, 3, 4, although Morphotype 4 can be referred most probably to a female.
source: Differently, the gender result difficult to infer for morphotypes 1, 2, 3, 4, although Morph. 4 can be referred most probably to a female.
evidence: Based on morphological analysis with uncertainty acknowledged

claim: Digitigrade and semi-plantigrade footprints provide information on pedal postures and the behavior of the producers passing through different sub-environments of the cave.
source: Digitigrade and semi-plantigrade footprints provide information on pedal postures and the behavior of the producers passing through different sub-environments of the cave.
evidence: Based on interpretation of different footprint types

claim: Both digitigrade and semi-plantigrade footprint types were, in most cases, traced back to the same type of producer by comparison with complete footprints indicating complete foot support during locomotion.
source: Both these footprint types were, in most cases, traced back to the same type of producer by comparison with complete footprints indicating complete foot support during locomotion.
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of footprint types

claim: Some semi-plantigrade footprints show a strongly adducted trace of digit I and an apparent alignment with the other digits, probably because of the intra-rotation movements of the distal portion of the foot during the thrust phase.
source: Some semi-plantigrade footprints (e.g. Figure 8, C44, C44b) show a strongly adducted trace of digit I and an apparent alignment with the other digits, probably because of the intra-rotation movements of the distal portion of the foot during the thrust phase.
evidence: Based on morphological observation and biomechanical interpretation

claim: Footprints included in Morphotype 3 show a peculiar pedal morphology with separation between digit pairs II-III and IV-V suggesting an inherited familiar trait or a pathological condition of the producer's feet.
source: Footprints included in the Morph. 3 show a peculiar pedal morphology. While the resulting morphology of the digit I trace is explained by walking on a waterlogged substrate, the separation between digit pairs II-III and IV-V suggest an inherited familiar trait or a pathological condition of the producer's feet.
evidence: Based on morphological analysis and interpretation of possible causes

claim: The producer of Morphotype 3 was not incapacitated, showing the greatest mobility in the hypogeal environment.
source: The producer was not incapacitated, showing the greatest mobility in the hypogeal environment.
evidence: Based on analysis of trackway patterns and distribution

claim: In the lower corridor, a few footprints are associated with elongated traces imprinted by the producers' knees resting on the substrate.
source: In the lower corridor (Figure 9), a few of these footprints are associated with elongated traces imprinted by the producers' knees resting on the substrate.
evidence: Supported by Figure 9 showing the traces

claim: Successions of kneeling traces can be clearly recognized for Morphotypes 3, 4, and 5.
source: Successions of kneeling traces can be clearly recognized for Morphs. 3, 4, and 5.
evidence: Based on analysis of trace patterns

claim: Based on the overall size of the metatarsal and knee couples aligned on the substrate, crawling in a totally unknown environment is inferred for the whole group.
source: Based on the overall size of the metatarsal and knee couples aligned on the substrate, crawling in a totally unknown environment is inferred for the whole group.
evidence: Based on analysis of trace patterns and spatial relationships

claim: Knee imprints show the muscle structure of the knee joint and adjacent regions, with recognizable patella, patellar ligament, tibial tuberosity, fibular head, basis of the vastus medial and the iliotibial band.
source: These knee imprints (e.g. Figure 8, C42) show the muscle structure of the knee joint and adjacent regions. The patella, the patellar ligament (tendon), the tibial tuberosity, the fibular head, the basis of the vastus medial and the iliotibial band are recognizable and allow us to infer the body structure of the trackmakers.
evidence: Based on detailed anatomical analysis of knee impressions shown in Figure 8

claim: Successions of kneeling traces allowing one to infer a crawling locomotion for the trackmakers have never been reported before.
source: Successions of kneeling traces allowing one to infer a crawling locomotion for the trackmakers have never been reported before.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Isolated kneeling traces have only previously been reported from the 'Galerie Wahl' at Fontanet cave and from the 'Salle des Talons' at Tuc d'Audoubert cave, France, but are not sufficient to infer crawling.
source: Isolated kneeling traces (i.e. a footprint followed by a knee imprint of the same leg) have only previously been reported from the 'Galerie Wahl' at Fontanet cave and from the 'Salle des Talons' at Tuc d'Audoubert cave, France (Pastoors et al., 2015) but are not sufficient to infer crawling.
evidence: Based on comparison with published reports from other caves

claim: The anatomic details clearly recognizable in the crawling traces from 'Grotta della Bàsura' enabled the hypothesis that no clothing was interposed between the limb and the trampled sediments.
source: In addition, the anatomic details clearly recognizable in the crawling traces from 'Grotta della Bàsura' enabled us to hypothesize that no clothing was interposed between the limb and the trampled sediments.
evidence: Based on inference from the level of anatomical detail preserved

claim: The short radiometric interval documented by both previous radiocarbon dates and those derived from the latest research, together with interferences relating to the interrelations of the different footprints, suggest that all individuals entered the cave at the same time.
source: The short radiometric interval, documented by both previous radiocarbon dates and those derived from the latest research presented here (Table 1), together with interferences relating to the interrelations of the different footprints, suggest that all individuals entered the cave at the same time.
evidence: Based on radiometric dating and analysis of footprint superposition patterns

claim: The group of footprints C34, C35b, C36, C35 in the terminal part of the 'Corridoio delle impronte' provides relative timing of the impressions, with C35 (Morphotype 4) superimposed on C36 (Morphotype 3) and on C34 and C35b (both Morphotype 5).
source: In particular, the group of footprints C34, C35b, C36, C35 in the terminal part of the 'Corridoio delle impronte' provides relative timing of the impressions: C35 (Morph. 4) is superimposed on C36 (Morph. 3) and on C34 and C35b (both Morph. 5) (Figure 9, d3).
evidence: Based on analysis of footprint superposition shown in Figure 9

claim: In the specific case of footprints C34-C36, the producer of Morphotype 4 passed after the producers of Morphotypes 3 and 5.
source: In this specific case, the producer of Morph. 4 passed after the producers of Morphs 3 and 5, respectively.
evidence: Based on analysis of footprint superposition

claim: In the entrance of the corridor, the timing is reversed: footprint C63 (Morphotype 4) is superimposed by C64 (Morphotype 3) proving that Morphotypes 3 and 4 were made at the same time.
source: In the entrance of the same corridor, the timing is reversed: footprint C63 (Morph. 4) is superimposed by C64 (Morph. 3) proving that Morphs. 3 and 4 were made at the same time (Figure 10).
evidence: Based on analysis of footprint superposition shown in Figure 10

claim: It is difficult to assume that Morphotypes 1 and 2 may have entered the deepest part of the cave without the presence of some older individual.
source: It is also difficult to assume that Morphs. 1 and 2 may have entered the deepest part of the cave without the presence of some older individual: if the older individuals who were leading the exploration were either Morphs. 3 or 4 the group consequently increases to include at least four individuals.
evidence: Based on logical inference about group composition and behavior

claim: All the available lines of evidence strongly suggest that a single exploration event by a heterogeneous group of five individuals is the most parsimonious and best supported hypothesis.
source: Thus, all the available lines of evidence, particularly the complex interrelationship of the studied footprints, strongly suggest that a single exploration event by a heterogeneous group of five individuals is the most parsimonious and best supported hypothesis.
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple lines of evidence

claim: Five individuals, comprising two adults, an adolescent and two children, entered the cave barefoot and with a set of Pinus t. sylvestris/mugo bundles which were burned for illumination purposes.
source: Five individuals, comprising two adults, an adolescent and two children, entered the cave barefoot and with a set of Pinus t. sylvestris/mugo bundles which were burned for illumination purposes.
evidence: Based on synthesis of footprint analysis, age estimation, and charcoal identification

claim: The adopted lighting system of several sticks enabled a longer period of lighting, as inferred from the fire wood illumination bundles adopted by the Bronze age salt miners at Hallstatt.
source: The adopted lighting system of several sticks enabled a longer period of lighting, as inferred from the fire wood illumination bundles adopted by the Bronze age salt miners at Hallstatt (Grabner et al., 2007; Grabner et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on analogy with documented Bronze Age practices

claim: Lighting bundles were usually made of resinous wood (Scots pine or Mountain pine), and called torch wood.
source: Lighting bundles were usually made of resinous wood (Scots pine or Mountain pine), and called torch wood (Ast, 2001; Théry-Parisot et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ancient lighting practices

claim: After a walk of approximately 150 m from the original opening of the cave and a climb of about 12 m, the group arrived at the 'Corridoio delle impronte'.
source: After a walk of approximately 150 m from the original opening of the cave and a climb of about 12 m, the group arrived at the 'Corridoio delle impronte'.
evidence: Based on cave topography measurements

claim: The group proceeded roughly in single file, with the smallest individual behind, and walked very close to the side wall of the cave.
source: They proceeded roughly in single file, with the smallest individual behind, and walked very close to the side wall of the cave, a safer approach also used by other animals (e.g. Canidae incertae sedis and bears) when moving in a poorly lit and unknown environment.
evidence: Based on analysis of trackway patterns and comparison with animal behavior

claim: The slope of the tunnel floor, inclined by about 24°, may have further forced the individuals to proceed along the only flat area in the lower corridor, a couple of meters from the left wall of the cave.
source: The slope of the tunnel floor, inclined by about 24°, may have further forced the individuals to proceed along the only flat area in the lower corridor, a couple of meters from the left wall of the cave.
evidence: Based on topographic measurements and inference about movement constraints

claim: About 10 m from the 'Corridoio delle impronte', the cave roof drops to below 80 cm and members of the group were forced to crawl, placing their hands and knees on the clay substrate.
source: About 10 m from the 'Corridoio delle impronte', the cave roof drops to below 80 cm and members of the group were forced to crawl (Figure 11B), placing their hands (Figure 12) and knees (Figure 8b) on the clay substrate (Figure 9) (see also Video 1).
evidence: Based on cave topography measurements and trace evidence shown in figures

claim: The group leader stopped, impressing two parallel calcigrade footprints, possibly to decide on the next movement and proceeded to cross the parts where the cave roof was at its lowest.
source: After a few meters, the group leader stopped, impressing two parallel calcigrade footprints, possibly to decide on the next movement and proceeded to cross the parts where the cave roof was at its lowest.
evidence: Based on analysis of footprint patterns and inference about behavior

claim: The other individuals also stopped at the same place as the leader, and then proceeded along the same path by crawling and following the group leader.
source: The other individuals also stopped at the same place as the leader, and then proceeded along the same path by crawling and following the group leader, as indicated by the timing reconstructed from interactions between the tracks (Figure 9, d3).
evidence: Based on analysis of footprint superposition and spatial patterns

claim: After passing a bottleneck of blocks and stalagmites, the party descended for about ten meters along a steeply sloping surface.
source: After passing a bottleneck of blocks and stalagmites, the party descended for about ten meters along a steeply sloping surface.
evidence: Based on cave topography and trackway analysis

claim: The whole group traversed a small pond, leaving deep tracks on the plastic waterlogged substrate, climbed a slope of 10 m beyond the 'Cimitero degli orsi', and finally arrived at the terminal room 'Sala dei Misteri', where they stopped.
source: The whole group traversed a small pond, leaving deep tracks on the plastic waterlogged substrate, climbed a slope of 10 m beyond the 'Cimitero degli orsi', and finally arrived at the terminal room 'Sala dei Misteri', where they stopped.
evidence: Based on trackway analysis and cave topography

claim: On the walls, several charcoal traces, generated by the torches, are preserved.
source: On the walls, several charcoal traces, generated by the torches, are preserved.
evidence: Based on observation of charcoal marks

claim: Some charcoal handprints produced by a flexed reaching up more than 170 cm on the roof of the 'Sala dei Misteri' confirm that the tallest individuals (Morphotypes 4 and 5) were able to touch this part of the gallery.
source: Some charcoal handprints produced by a flexed reaching up more than 170 cm on the roof of the 'Sala dei Misteri' confirm that the tallest individuals (Morphs. 4 and 5) were able to touch this part of the gallery.
evidence: Based on measurement of handprint height and comparison with stature estimates

claim: The fact that footprints of the tallest individuals are not preserved in the central portion of the hall relates to the loss of the central portion of the hall floor.
source: The fact that their footprints are not preserved relates to the loss of the central portion of the hall floor.
evidence: Based on inference about preservation and erosion

claim: In the 'Sala dei Misteri', the adolescent and children started collecting clay from the floor and smeared it on a stalagmite at different levels according to height, as suggested by the breadth and relative distribution of the finger flutings on the karst structure.
source: In the same room, the adolescent and children started collecting clay from the floor and smeared it on a stalagmite at different levels according to height, as suggested by the breadth and relative distribution of the finger flutings on the karst structure.
evidence: Based on analysis of finger fluting patterns and inference about behavior

claim: During their sojourn in the innermost room of the cave the young individual that produced Morphotype 2 imprinted ten clear heel traces, which are interpreted as calcigrade tracks produced by a trackmaker who is momentarily standing-still to excavate and manipulate clay.
source: During their sojourn in the innermost room of the cave the young individual, that produced Morph. 2, imprinted ten clear heel traces (Citton et al., 2017), which are here interpreted as calcigrade tracks produced by a trackmaker who is momentarily standing-still to excavate and manipulate clay as was also recorded for the 'Salle des Talons' at Tuc d'Audoubert cave (Pastoors et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on analysis of heel traces and comparison with similar behavior documented at another cave

claim: After stopping for several minutes, they exited and followed a route which did not always adhere to that followed on entry.
source: After stopping for several minutes (considering the quantity and ubiquity of the tracks), they exited and followed a route which did not always adhere to that followed on entry.
evidence: Based on analysis of trackway patterns and directions

claim: After passing the small pond, they crossed the upper corridor following a more comfortable and safer route.
source: After passing the small pond, they crossed the upper corridor following a more comfortable and safer route (Figure 11C).
evidence: Based on trackway analysis and cave topography shown in Figure 11C

claim: In the upper corridor all the prints point in the direction of the exit while in the lower corridor, with the axis of the foot oriented parallel to the walls, most of the footprints are directed toward the interior of the cave.
source: It is important to note that in the upper corridor all the prints point in the direction of the exit (Figures 11C and 13) while in the lower corridor, with the axis of the foot oriented parallel to the walls, most of the footprints are directed toward the interior of the cave.
evidence: Based on analysis of footprint orientations shown in figures

claim: The lower corridor was traversed on entry into the cave and documents the first unequivocal evidence of crawling locomotion in the human ichnological record.
source: The lower corridor was traversed on entry into the cave and documents the first unequivocal evidence of crawling locomotion in the human ichnological record.
evidence: Based on analysis of crawling traces and review of existing literature

claim: The crawling mode of locomotion was adopted by the explorers to obviate variation in the height of the cave roof.
source: This mode of locomotion was adopted by the explorers to obviate variation in the height of the cave roof.
evidence: Based on inference from cave topography and trace patterns

claim: As no outgoing footprints were documented in the lower corridor it appears that the group chose to exit through the upper corridor, as the cave roof is higher and the substrate firmer.
source: As no outgoing footprints were documented in the lower corridor it appears that the group chose to exit through the upper corridor, as the cave roof is higher and the substrate firmer.
evidence: Based on analysis of footprint directions and cave characteristics

claim: An additional reason for choosing the upper corridor path of exit could have been the exploratory and curiosity factor to follow a different and unexplored path to reach the cave exit.
source: An additional reason for choosing this path of exit could have been the exploratory and curiosity factor to follow a different and unexplored path to reach the cave exit.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of behavioral motivation

claim: Anatomical features clearly registered on the substrate indicate that the lower limbs of the individuals were not covered with clothing.
source: Anatomical features clearly registered on the substrate indicate that the lower limbs of the individuals were not covered with clothing.
evidence: Based on inference from the level of anatomical detail preserved in traces

claim: The study confirms that very young children actively participated in the activities of the Upper Palaeolithic populations, even in seemingly dangerous tasks, such as the deep exploration of the cave environment lit only with torches.
source: Our study also confirms that very young children actively participated in the activities of the Upper Palaeolithic populations, even in seemingly dangerous tasks, such as the deep exploration of the cave environment lit only with torches.
evidence: Based on synthesis of evidence showing presence of young children in the cave

claim: The 'Grotta della Bàsura' site strongly supports the hypothesis that the cave exploration in Upper Paleolithic was carried out by groups of heterogeneous age and gender.
source: As recently suggested for other European caves (Pastoors et al., 2015; Pastoors et al., 2017; Ledoux et al., 2017) the 'Grotta della Bàsura' site strongly supports the hypothesis that the cave exploration in Upper Paleolithic was carried out by groups of heterogeneous age and gender.
evidence: Based on synthesis of evidence and comparison with other cave sites

claim: The Epigravettian necropolis of the Arene Candide Cave consisted of a 'mixed' sample of people (males, females, adults, children) and suggests an Upper Palaeolithic people composition very similar to that highlighted in the 'Grotta della Bàsura'.
source: The Epigravettian necropolis of the Arene Candide Cave (AMS dates spanning 12,820–12,420 cal BP for the first phase and 12,030–11,180 cal BP for the second phase), consisted of a 'mixed' sample of people (males, females, adults, children) and suggests an Upper Palaeolithic people composition very similar to that highlighted in the 'Grotta della Bàsura' (Riel-Salvatore et al., 2018; Sparacello et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on comparison with published data from another site

claim: The burial of a newborn infant, together with grave goods, recently discovered in the Arma di Veirana cave indicates that women and children systematically followed the movements of the group in the territory.
source: The burial of a newborn infant, together with grave goods, recently discovered in the Arma di Veirana cave (Erli, Savona, Liguria) situated in a valley 10 km from the coast, further indicates that women and children systematically followed the movements of the group in the territory (F. N. pers. obs.) (Negrino et al., 2017)
evidence: Based on archaeological evidence from another site

claim: The tracks left in the Bàsura indicate that the behavior of hunter-gatherers was not always driven by subsistence requirements, but also by fun and frivolous activities.
source: The tracks left in the Bàsura indicate that the behavior of hunter-gatherers was not always driven by subsistence requirements, but as manifested by many ethnographic examples, also by fun and frivolous activities.
evidence: Based on interpretation of behavior and comparison with ethnographic data

claim: Radiometric dating of charcoals previously established the presence of humans in the cave to the Upper Palaeolithic, around 12,340 ± 160 years BP.
source: Radiometric dating of charcoals previously established the presence of humans in the cave to the Upper Palaeolithic, around 12,340 ± 160 years BP (De Lumley and Giacobini, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous radiometric dating study

claim: The stalagmite crust preserving the footprints and incorporating fragments of coal is dated to between 14,300 ± 800 and 13,100 ± 500.
source: The stalagmite crust preserving the footprints and incorporating fragments of coal is dated to between 14,300 ± 800 and 13,100 ± 500 (Yokoyama et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to radiometric dating study

claim: The final phase of stalagmite growth, which closed the entrance and sealed the 'time capsule', occurred at 12,000 ± 1100.
source: The final phase of stalagmite growth, which closed the entrance and sealed the 'time capsule', occurred at 12,000 ± 1100 (Yokoyama et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to radiometric dating study

claim: New radiometric dating of charcoal samples of Pinus t. sylvestris/mugo was undertaken in 2017 at an AMS facility at Groningen.
source: New radiometric dating of charcoal samples of Pinus t. sylvestris/mugo was undertaken in 2017 at a AMS facility at Groningen (NL) on (Table 1).
evidence: Describes new dating work with results in Table 1

claim: Material for new dating was collected from the trampled palaeosurface during recent excavations inside the 'Sala dei Misteri'.
source: Material was collected from the trampled palaeosurface during recent excavations inside the 'Sala dei Misteri' (Figure 14).
evidence: Describes sampling methodology shown in Figure 14

claim: The main landmarks of the cave were digitally recorded using the laser scanner ScanStation2 Leica and ScanStation C10 Leica.
source: The main landmarks of the cave were digitally recorded using the laser scanner ScanStation2 Leica and ScanStation C10 Leica.
evidence: Describes methodology for 3D documentation

claim: In total, 23 stations were run (nine in the 'Sala dei Misteri' and 14 in the 'Corridoio delle impronte' areas) with 38 targets used for the point clouds registration.
source: In total, 23 stations were run (nine in the 'Sala dei Misteri' and 14 in the 'Corridoio delle impronte' areas); 38 targets (16 in the 'Sala dei misteri' and 22 in the 'Corridoio delle impronte') were used for the point clouds registration.
evidence: Describes technical details of laser scanning methodology

claim: The laser scanning recording shows a final alignment error of 2 mm for the model of the 'Sala dei Misteri' and 1 mm for the 'Corridoio delle impronte'.
source: The recording shows a final alignment error of 2 mm for the model of the 'Sala dei Misteri' and 1 mm for the 'Corridoio delle impronte' (Video 1).
evidence: Provides precision metrics for 3D models

claim: The original casts performed in 1950 were digitally acquired via HDI Advance structured-light 3D Scanner R3x, with a resolution of 0.25 mm at 600 mm FOV.
source: The original cast performed in 1950 were digitally acquired via HDI Advance structured-light 3D Scanner R3x, with a resolution of 0.25 mm at 600 mm FOV (field of view).
evidence: Describes methodology for digitizing historical casts

claim: All recognized tracks (107 human traces) were analyzed directly in the field through a morphological approach using available landmarks.
source: All recognized tracks (107 human traces) were analyzed directly in the field through a morphological approach using available landmarks (Robbins, 1985).
evidence: Describes methodology for footprint analysis

claim: All footprints identified during the early explorations are still visible in situ.
source: Their positions in the cave were verified and it was established that all the footprints identified during the early explorations are still visible in situ (Figure 1, Table 4).
evidence: Based on verification of historical records against current observations

claim: Some footprints have suffered alteration and loss of detail and others have been partially damaged.
source: Some of them have suffered alteration and loss of detail and others have been partially damaged.
evidence: Based on assessment of preservation state

claim: In some instances, morphometric data of the in situ footprints were integrated with those of plaster casts.
source: For this reason, in some instances, we have integrated morphometric data of the in situ footprints with those of plaster casts.
evidence: Describes methodological approach to data collection

claim: The 23 better preserved footprints were subjected to a Principal Component Analysis using the software PAST 3.10.
source: The 23 better preserved footprints were subjected to a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using the software PAST 3.10 (Hammer et al., 2001).
evidence: Describes statistical analysis methodology

claim: The raw data were log-transformed before the analysis to fit linear models and for the correspondence of the log transform to an isometric null hypothesis.
source: The raw data were log-transformed before the analysis to fit linear models and for the correspondence of the log transform to an isometric null hypothesis (Chinnery, 2004; Cheng et al., 2009; Romano and Citton, 2015; Romano and Citton, 2017; Romano, 2017).
evidence: Describes data transformation methodology with supporting citations

claim: It is possible to estimate stature from foot length.
source: It is possible to estimate stature from foot length (Robbins, 1985; Oberoi et al., 2006; Krishan and Sharma, 2007; Kanchan et al., 2008; Pawar and Pawar, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established methods

claim: Based on skeletal evidence, it is thought that the body proportions of terminal Upper Palaeolithic individuals was similar to that of modern humans.
source: Based on skeletal evidence, it is thought that the body proportions of terminal Upper Palaeolithic individuals was similar to that of modern humans (Trinkaus, 1997; Ruff et al., 2005; Shackelford, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to skeletal studies

claim: The foot length/stature ratio for terminal Upper Palaeolithic individuals was considered highly uncertain, between 0.15 and 0.16.
source: but the foot length/stature ratio was considered highly uncertain, between 0.15 and 0.16.
evidence: Based on existing knowledge with acknowledged uncertainty

claim: The calculated foot length/stature ratio based on a sample of terminal Upper Palaeolithic adult individuals (n.8) from the Italian Peninsula is 0.1541.
source: Consequently, we calculated the foot length/stature ratio based on a sample of terminal Upper Palaeolithic adult individuals (n.8) from the Italian Peninsula (Corrain, 1977; Paoli et al., 1980; Formicola et al., 1990; Mallegni and Fabbri, 1995; Mallegni et al., 2000). The calculated ratio is found to be 0.1541
evidence: Based on calculation from published skeletal data

claim: The calculated ratio of 0.1541 is close to those proposed for modern humans between the XIX and XX centuries.
source: The calculated ratio is found to be 0.1541, which is close to those proposed for modern humans between the XIX and XX centuries (Robbins, 1985; Topinard, 1878).
evidence: Based on comparison with historical data

claim: The percutaneous length of the tibia is known to have a strong correlation with body height.
source: In this study, we used the percutaneous length of the tibia to check the stature of the Morph. 5 as this measurement is known to have a strong correlation with body height.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: For a tibial length of 35 cm, the stature of Morphotype 5 is 165.2 ± 3.73 cm, which is comparable to the stature assumed from foot length (166.99 ± 2.93 cm).
source: For a tibial length of 35 cm, the stature of Morph. 5 is 165.2 ± 3.73 cm, which is comparable to the stature assumed from foot length (166.99 ± 2.93 cm).
evidence: Based on calculation using established formula and comparison of methods

claim: Body mass estimates were derived from footprint parameters, based on the assumption that human body proportions have been constant through time.
source: Body mass estimates were derived from footprint parameters, based on the assumption that human body proportions have been constant through time (Dingwall et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on cited methodology with stated assumption

claim: Studies on the relationship size/age of the foot in extant juvenile individuals have highlighted that 1-year-old individuals have a foot length equal to 13.07 ± 1.59 cm, reaching 24.4 ± 2.96 cm at the age of 13 years.
source: Studies on the relationship size/age of the foot in extant juvenile individuals (Fryar et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2012) have highlighted that 1-year-old individuals have a foot length equal to 13.07 ± 1.59 cm, reaching 24.4 ± 2.96 cm at the age of 13 years.
evidence: Supported by citations to growth studies

claim: Anthropometric studies suggest that the morphology of the foot changes and becomes more elongated when the arch stabilizes around the age of six.
source: Anthropometric studies suggest that the morphology of the foot changes and becomes more elongated when the arch stabilizes around the age of six (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to developmental study

claim: In extant human populations, from the fifth or sixth years of age, arch angles vary from 21° (3–4 years) to 43° (9–11 years) in young males, and from 26° (3–4 years) to 47° (9–11 years) in young females.
source: In extant human populations, from the fifth or sixth years of age, arch angles vary from 21° (3–4 years) to 43° (9–11 years) in young males, and from 26° (3–4 years) to 47° (9–11 years) in young females (Forriol and Pascual, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to developmental study

claim: Sex determination established from the foot has been proposed using Foot index and threshold values, but this approach is not entirely accepted.
source: Sex determination established from the foot has been proposed using Foot index and threshold values. However, this approach is not entirely accepted and some researchers pointed out that the threshold value could vary significantly between populations, thus making it very speculative that gender estimations could be determined from foot morphology (Walia et al., 2016).
evidence: Describes method with acknowledged limitations from cited literature

claim: Variations in foot anatomy could be due to the fact that anatomic structures of the foot manifest ethnic and regional variations owing to climatic factors, physical activities, socio-economic status and nutritional conditions.
source: These variations could be due to fact that anatomic structures of the foot manifest ethnic and regional variations owing to climatic factors, physical activities, socio-economic status and nutritional conditions.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of factors affecting foot morphology
